The Purple-throated Carib (Eulampis jugularis) exhibits a striking sexual dimorphism in adult body mass, a pattern commonly observed among hummingbirds where males and females occupy slightly different foraging niches. Adult females of this species typically reach an ultimate wet weight of 8.5 grams [Wwi = 8.5 grams], whereas males attain a larger adult body mass of 10.5 grams [Wwi = 10.5 grams], a difference of nearly 24 percent. This size disparity is thought to be linked to male-male competition for access to territories rich in Heliconia flowers, where larger body size confers an advantage in aerial chases and aggressive displays. In contrast, the smaller size of females may facilitate greater maneuverability during the complex hovering maneuvers required to extract nectar from flowers with curved corollas, a task that also demands considerable energetic expenditure. The dimorphism is not merely a static trait but reflects divergent selective pressures acting on each sex across their respective life histories. At the other end of the size spectrum, neonates emerge from their eggs at a remarkably modest initial weight of 1.1 grams [Wwb = 1.1 grams], based on scaling relationships observed in a closely related congener, Doryfera ludovicae. This tiny hatchling mass, equivalent to roughly one-tenth of the adult female's weight, underscores the high degree of parental investment required to rear offspring to independence.

The incubation period and early developmental milestones of Eulampis jugularis are tightly coupled to thermal conditions within the nest. Eggs incubated at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] hatch after approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days], a developmental duration that is typical for a hummingbird of this body size but which may vary by a day or two depending on microclimatic fluctuations within the montane forest understory. The relatively prolonged incubation, characteristic of birds with such elevated metabolic rates, reflects the substantial investment females make in each reproductive attempt. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on maternal provisioning for thermoregulation and nutrition, growing rapidly on a diet of regurgitated arthropods and nectar. The nestling period, during which the chick remains confined to the cup nest and receives all meals from the attending parent, culminates in fledging at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching], measured at the typical body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] that characterizes active metabolism in this species. This fledging age marks the point at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight, a critical transition from a stationary, brooded existence to a mobile, albeit still partially dependent, life in the canopy.

Pubertal development in the Purple-throated Carib proceeds in a clearly delineated sequence following a period of juvenile growth. Under the standard thermal regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] that defines the active metabolic state of this species, the gonads become fully mature at 58 days after hatching [tp = 58 days after hatching], a relatively rapid progression compared to many passerines of similar adult mass. This accelerated onset of sexual maturation allows young birds to quickly integrate into the local breeding population, a strategy that may be adaptive in unpredictable nectar environments where high reproductive turnover can buffer against stochastic year-class failures. Despite this early physiological pubertal milestone, first reproduction is not immediately initiated; females typically defer their first successful clutch until 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], also measured at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. The pronounced lag between gonadal maturity and actual breeding activity is ecologically significant, as it provides a full year for territory acquisition, refinement of foraging skills in complex floral habitats, and accumulation of sufficient body condition to sustain the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. This life-history pattern places the species among those that invest heavily in a single, well-timed annual reproductive event.

The metabolic machinery underlying this species' active life is impressive and has been quantified through controlled respirometry trials. Basal oxygen consumption, reflecting the minimal energetic cost of maintaining vital physiological functions at rest, reaches 69.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 69.5 milliliters per hour] at 38.1 °C, measured at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This elevated resting metabolic rate is commensurate with the extreme hovering capabilities and rapid wing-beat frequencies that characterize the Trochilidae, yet it falls within the expected range for a bird of this body mass. The rate is particularly remarkable when scaled against the species' small size, as mass-specific metabolic demands in hummingbirds are among the highest recorded for any endotherm. This aerobic capacity enables sustained foraging bouts on energy-rich nectar, but it also imposes a high daily energy budget that drives the species' reliance on torpor on cold nights to conserve fuel reserves. Regarding reproductive output, females lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a conservative reproductive strategy that contrasts sharply with the high metabolism that otherwise defines this species' physiology.

Longevity records for the Purple-throated Carib indicate that individuals in the wild can survive for approximately 7.5 years [am = approximately 7.5 years], when maintained at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a lifespan that places it among the longer-lived hummingbirds given its small size. This extended survival is likely facilitated by the species' relatively low predation risk in the dense montane forests of the Lesser Antilles, combined with a high-quality nectar diet that supports consistent somatic condition. Interestingly, the age-specific mortality patterns do not show a sharp increase immediately following reproductive senescence, suggesting that physiological deterioration is gradual rather than catastrophic in this taxon. The maximum longevity documented in banding studies approaches 8 years in some island populations, though the rigorous energetic demands of daily hovering flight and nocturnal torpor cycles may impose a ceiling on attainable age. Few species of comparable body mass achieve such lifespans, a fact that highlights the interplay between slow reproductive rates, low extrinsic mortality, and the metabolic constraints of being the smallest of endotherms. The species thus exemplifies a life-history strategy that balances high metabolic throughput with surprisingly slow reproductive and aging schedules, a combination that underscores the remarkable diversity of avian life-history evolution within the Neotropics.
